title: Improvising in the 1920s: Cuban Bennett and paraphrase versus chorus phrase
summary: Carter says Cuban Bennett first ran changes, and discusses paraphrase and chorus phrase improvisation.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, let me ask one other thing that maybe we can come full circle with through various channels.
Uh huh?
You mentioned just a little while ago that there were a number of fine improvisers in the 1920's.
Uh huh.
When you were coming up. Yet, a

number of the records I've listened to that the solos, or what we would think of, when we only hear one take of something; we now have the luxury of hearing 2 or 3 takes, maybe recorded on the same date, or 2 or 3 different versions of the same piece that had been recorded in a short period of time -- maybe only a month or two months away from each other.
Uh huh.

And quite often, the solos are the things that we would think, if we only heard one version, would think were improvised. Indeed, we're not. I mean, they're very, very close to each other. This happens on a number of early Duke Ellington things, even indeed, with Bubber Bubba Miley and so forth -- the famous case of the Dipper Mouth solo, which was a set solo.

So I was just wondering -- I don't want to make a great deal out of just those few examples, but if there really was that much improvising, if improvising was ... I don't know quite how to put it ... as much a part of the jazzman's trade back then as it was now, what -- now, I think we assume that most people that we call 'jazzmen' are very, very capable improvisers. Was that the case then?

Yes, I think ... it's a pity that I don't ... well, I won't say that I don't, just -- that none of us have any examples of the playing of a trumpet player named Cuban Bennett, who was a first cousin of mine, and he was the first one that I think -- and Roy Eldridge Eldridge, who may be one
of the few people around who would remember him -- Roy Eldridge Ordige would attest to this -- he was probably the first musician that we heard that ran as we called it -- changes -- you know?
Uh huh.
He had a great sound and he had a -- he heard everything, and played everything, you know? I don't know if I'm ...
overestimating the case, or ...

No. I'm not overestimating the case, but if I'm trying to show the relationship of what he did what we would call improvisation -- maybe I misunderstood the point you were trying to make when you said about the musicians back in the 20's; the things you've heard, and what was that again?
Well, I'm just wondering if ...

I don't know quite how to put this, but the level of improvisation was as extensive then as it has become since. Were there as many capable improvisors who were called jazz musicians as there are now?

Well, there certainly weren't as many; it's just that they played differently. What they were playing .... if you play a solo and you -- like if you were to play the "St. Louis Blues" , you'd go da dee doo da, but if you said da da dee doo da, da, -- well this is still improvising. Very simply, and you're not running a great deal of changed, but it's still -- you're improvising or
to some degree, you're certainly altering the melody. Would that be synonymous with improvising?
Well, it brings in to question here, two terms that I guess were coined again by Andre Hodier, which he calls the paraphrase, which is what you're describing.
Yes, yes, yes.
And then what he calls the 'chorus phrase' which is, as you described before, running changes. That's ignoring the given melody.
Uh huh. Right. Ignoring it indeed. But just improvising on the same chord structure.

Indeed. Now when in your memory, did --what Hodier would call a chorus phrase -- improvising become a more standard method of improvising or a more standard method of improvised variation in jazz music?
You mentioned Cuban Bennett as being the first one that you can recall in this technique.
Yes, and that was certainly in the 20's -- the early 20's. I don't know ... I would say probably the early 20's -- late 20's.
